title: Northshore Health - Onprem Airgapped Discovery
summary: Intro discovery focused on Northshore's air-gapped on-prem requirements. Covered update process for offline environments, hardware constraints (GPU types, rack density), compliance needs (SOC2, audit logs, KMS/HSM integration), latency vs cost tradeoffs, and pilot success criteria. Agreed next steps: send security pack, schedule deep-dive workshop, propose hardware checklist and pilot SOW.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (CTO, Northshore), Dr. Lena Ortiz (CISO), Ravi Kapoor (ML Eng), Tamara Blake (Procurement)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to validate on-prem, air-gapped constraints and next steps for pilot.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, uh, really appreciate it. I'm Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Mark Reynolds: Good, thanks Jordan. Busy week but excited to chat.
[00:17] Priya Patel: Hi all, quick agenda — understand your environment, constraints around air-gap and patching, hardware, and what a successful pilot looks like.
[00:27] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Perfect. From security perspective — this is all about data residency and no egress, we need to be fully air-gapped, and any update process must be approved.
[00:36] Jordan Lee: Totally, that's clear. Maybe start high level — can you run through the cluster and where you see Redwood fitting?
[00:44] Mark Reynolds: Sure. We have a primary on-prem DC in Boston, backup in Rochester, both isolated from internet. Our ML infra is a mix — some older 2080/Tesla V100s and we've been evaluating M60 to A10s; vendor approvals are finicky. We want inference to be local for latency and PHI concerns.
[01:06] Ravi Kapoor: Also, per compliance, models can't call home. Updates must be pushed via approved media or jump box workflows.
[01:14] Priya Patel: Understood. For air-gapped we support offline bundles and signed packages — practically, how do you envision updates? USB or physically seeding a jumpbox, or an internal repo?
[01:25] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Ideally via an internal repo. But in practice procurement often requires a physically delivered package for initial install, then we can mirror it behind the firewall. All binaries must be signed, and we need reproducible checksums.
[01:38] Jordan Lee: That's consistent with other regulated customers. We have a private deployment that runs entirely on your network, supports offline install, and can integrate with your KMS or an HSM. Question on KMS: do you have an HSM vendor already?
[01:52] Dr. Lena Ortiz: We have Thales and a Cohort of YubiHSM in staging. The legal team prefers Thales.
[01:58] Priya Patel: Good — Redwood can integrate with external HSMs via PKCS#11 for key wrapping. There may be some extra steps for signing update bundles to align with your internal CI/CD gating.
[02:10] Ravi Kapoor: What about model updates? We do frequent model refreshes — weekly experiments — but production models change less often. We need a way to push new model files without creating a network egress risk.
[02:23] Jordan Lee: We typically package model artifacts as encrypted model bundles signed by your key. You can import them through the offline bundle flow. For heavy models we also support chunked import to avoid timeouts.
[02:33] Mark Reynolds: Latency is also a concern. Some of our endpoints require sub-100ms response. Can Redwood meet that on your hardware?
[02:41] Priya Patel: It depends on model size and batch strategy. For generation use-cases with smaller seq lengths and continuous batching disabled, we've seen 50–80ms on A10/A100-class GPUs per token for optimized quantized models. For large context models you'll see higher latencies. We can recommend quantized variants to balance cost and latency.
[03:01] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Speaking of quantization — from a validation standpoint we need to ensure there is no regression in clinical accuracy. How do you help with quality monitoring?
[03:10] Priya Patel: Redwood Optimize includes evaluation hooks and can run prompt-based regression tests tied to alerting. For private deployments we hand over the eval harness and can run a baseline locally with your test set.
[03:21] Mark Reynolds: On the procurement side — Tamara, any constraints on vendor certifications?
[03:25] Tamara Blake: We usually need SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 for any software vendor with access to systems. Air-gapped makes it easier but we still require attestations and an executed BA agreement for PHI. Also need a standard SOW for pilot costs.
[03:40] Jordan Lee: We can provide SOC2, ISO docs, and we've done BAAs with other health systems. I'll send the pack after this call.
[03:48] Ravi Kapoor: One technical thing — our rack density and power limits: we can't exceed 3kW per rack; thermal is a constraint. Which GPUs do you support for private installs?
[03:59] Priya Patel: We support A10, A30, A100, and some customers run Ampere-based options. For tight power/thermal constraints, we often recommend multi-node smaller GPUs with model parallelism or model sharding, or quantized CPU fallbacks, though CPU inference will be slower. We can help size the cluster.
[04:18] Mark Reynolds: Firmware patching is another headache. We maintain a strict firmware baseline; vendor-drops can block us. How much control do we have over runtime upgrades?
[04:27] Jordan Lee: You retain full control. Redwood's private control plane runs on a management node that can be air-gapped as well; you control when to apply service updates. We provide signed update bundles and a test harness to validate against your firmware baseline in staging.
[04:40] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Audit logs are mandatory. We need immutable logs for all key operations and access traces. Retention is at least seven years for some flows.
[04:49] Priya Patel: We can configure audit log retention locally and integrate with your SIEM via syslog or file drop. For immutability we support WORM-like patterns if your storage stack supports it.
[05:00] Tamara Blake: Pricing — are we looking at a subscription or one-time license for private?
[05:05] Jordan Lee: For Private we do license + support fees. For Dedicated we do reserved capacity. For private on-prem it's typically a per-instance license plus support/maintenance and optional professional services. We'll get finance to provide a draft SOW after the pilot scope is agreed.
[05:18] Mark Reynolds: What would a pilot look like, timeline-wise?
[05:22] Priya Patel: Usually 6–8 weeks: week 1–2 is install and validation, week 3–4 is workload testing and eval, week 5–6 is performance tuning and handover. For air-gapped sites the install time can be longer due to procurement and media transport.
[05:36] Ravi Kapoor: For the install we need a hardware checklist. Are there strict OS/kernel versions Redwood expects?
[05:42] Priya Patel: We publish a supported OS matrix; common ones are Ubuntu 20.04/22.04 with specific kernel patches for NVIDIA drivers. We'll include exact driver versions and container runtime requirements in the checklist.
[05:55] Jordan Lee: Anything else from security?
[05:57] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Two more items — SSO/SAML integration with our IdP for RBAC, and role separation so ops can't trigger model updates without approvals.
[06:07] Priya Patel: We support SAML SSO and granular RBAC hooks; for change control we can gate updates behind an approval workflow that ties to your ticketing system.
[06:16] Mark Reynolds: On performance — we also want to run a head-to-head benchmark vs our in-house runtime. Will Redwood run a benchmark plan?
[06:23] Jordan Lee: Yes, Priya can run an on-prem benchmark with your test set as part of the workshop. We'll produce token-level latency and cost estimates.
[06:31] Ravi Kapoor: A practical detail — network egress: our jump box only allows outbound to a whitelisted internal repo. Will Redwood's offline installer work with a local Yum/Apt proxy?
[06:40] Priya Patel: Yes, the installer supports internal repos and proxies. For packages we can ship RPMs or DEBs and a signed manifest.
[06:48] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Good. Also need proof of encryption in transit — TLS mutual auth for any management plane connections.
[06:55] Priya Patel: We support mTLS for control plane communications; all management endpoints can be configured behind your VPN and only accept cert-based auth.
[07:04] Tamara Blake: On contracts — do you require inbound network access to validate license keys? That's a procurement red flag for us.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: No, we can validate licenses offline; we support signed license files that can be provisioned manually.
[07:18] Mark Reynolds: Great. What about day-2 ops — monitoring and alerting?
[07:22] Priya Patel: For Private we ship a self-hosted metrics stack optionally, or integrate with your Prometheus/Grafana. We also provide tracing hooks and token-level cost dashboards in the console; for air-gapped installs the console can be run inside your network.
[07:35] Ravi Kapoor: Any limits on concurrent sessions or API rate limits for private?
[07:39] Jordan Lee: Those are configurable per deployment. We often set default quotas but you can tune them to match throughput and hardware capacity.
[07:47] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Ok risk question — if there's a vulnerability in a model or runtime that needs urgent patching, what's the emergency path?
[07:55] Priya Patel: We have an incident response playbook. For air-gapped customers we provide signed emergency patch bundles and recommended mitigations. We also coordinate with your security team to validate and stage the patch.
[08:06] Tamara Blake: Who handles PII/PHI breach notification?
[08:09] Jordan Lee: Contractually Redwood will follow the agreed notification timelines; we can include specific SLAs in the BAA.
[08:16] Mark Reynolds: Financially, if we go to pilot, what's the expected cost range?
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Pilot professional services typically range 25–50k depending on scope and onsite support. License evaluation copies can be provided for the pilot window.
[08:30] Ravi Kapoor: A few small clarifications — do you do model quantization in-place or do we need to produce separate quantized models?
[08:36] Priya Patel: We can provide tooling to quantize models as part of the pipeline and store quantized model artifacts. We also support on-the-fly quantized execution paths for supported architectures. There are tradeoffs we'll quantify in the bench.
[08:50] Mark Reynolds: Ok, risk register items for us are procurement lead time, firmware/driver alignment, and validation of clinical accuracy.
[08:59] Jordan Lee: Noted. We'll include those in the pilot SOW.
[09:04] Priya Patel: Next practical step — we propose an on-prem workshop next week where we walk through the installer, run a small smoke test, and collect metrics. Would next Tuesday work?
[09:13] Tamara Blake: Procurement needs to check but tentatively yes, next Tuesday is fine.
[09:18] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Security team will need a pre-call to review the installer process.
[09:22] Jordan Lee: Great — we'll arrange a short pre-call just with security. Jordan and Priya will follow up with calendar invites.
[09:29] Mark Reynolds: Anything else from Redwood?
[09:31] Jordan Lee: I'll send the security pack, SOC2, and a high-level deployment diagram after this call. Priya will send the hardware checklist and proposed bench plan.
[09:40] Priya Patel: And we'll include driver/kernel versions and a minimal supported OS matrix.
[09:44] Tamara Blake: Sounds good. We'll share the procurement windows and internal vendor approval process.
[09:49] Jordan Lee: Cool. Quick recap of action items and owners — we'll follow up in email. Thanks everyone.
[09:56] Mark Reynolds: Thanks, talk soon.
[09:58] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Thanks all.

Notes on transcript quality: Some words may be mis-transcribed (firmware vendor names, kernel versions). There was occasional crosstalk.

End of call.
